P11r1: The problem is that, in a group of eight people, if two are in a sustained crisis mode, the group may end up spending most of its attention caring for those in crisis. However, in a group of eighty people, the same need can often be spread across lots of relationships and roles. A group can only absorb as much need as its members have free resource to meet.

P13n1: There is a difficult paradox to consider. The need for new members in a small community is greater, but the ability of that community to tolerate the disruption of new members is less. Whether there are eight people in the community or eight hundred, someone still has to grow the food, fix the equipment, balance the books, watch the kids, and maintain the water system. The water well doesn’t care how beautiful a new member’s heart is.
P15n2: How to use the framing of “I don’t have the capacity to…” without it becoming a respectable way to exclude disabled people, poor people, people who aren’t very articulate or don’t have the language of therapy at their fingertips, people who are simply not convenient – I don’t know. It’s not going to be solved by pretending it’s unlimited; that’s going to require actually making concrete criteria, allowing for outside review, allowing for re-visiting a “not now” decision, and all of that. And even then, the power is dangerous.

P2c: This does not surprise me, since we are taught to put on a show of competence in modern society. We have a lot of incentives to hide ourselves in our lives and disappear behind our screens the second things get uncomfortable. We have been encouraged by our institutions to be narrow in our skills, and then they act surprised that when a conflict comes up, all anyone knows how to do is appoint a subcommittee or just hit block.
